title: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
content:
It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design. The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It’s under Activity in the Gemini settings. You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.
Importantly, this only applies to future interactions with Gemini. If you have previously fed any data into Google’s AI, that’s already part of the training data. That can include your inputs, Gemini’s responses, uploaded files, tool calls, your location, and data from connected apps. Google says it may retain this data for up to three years to improve its models. The company has previously noted it attempts to filter personal information out of the Gemini activity history, but that isn’t a guarantee.

report.summary: Google now lets Gemini users opt out of AI training while keeping their chat history, splitting two controls that were previously locked together.
report.background: Gemini is woven through Google's products — Search, Workspace, Android — and every conversation feeds the company's model-improvement pipeline. Until now, Google tied two things together: excluding your chats from training meant disabling Gemini Apps Activity entirely, which also destroyed your ability to resume conversations later. That all-or-nothing design drew criticism from privacy advocates and regulators, especially in Europe, where GDPR and the Digital Markets Act push for granular, data-minimizing choices rather than take-it-or-leave-it consent. Rivals including OpenAI and Anthropic already separate training controls from history retention, and Apple has leaned heavily on privacy marketing for Apple Intelligence. Google's change reflects both competitive pressure and a maturing regulatory climate in which bundling unrelated data uses into a single switch is increasingly scrutinized.
key_points: Google is splitting one setting into two: a chat history toggle that controls whether you can revisit past conversations, and a separate AI training toggle that controls whether Google learns from them. Previously, opting out of training required deleting your history, so privacy-conscious users lost continuity and context.

Training remains opt-out, not opt-in. You must actively find and disable the toggle under Gemini settings > Activity, or via your Google account at Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity. Default behavior for most users does not change.

The change is not retroactive. Anything you already sent to Gemini — prompts, responses, uploads, tool calls, location data, connected-app data — is already in the training pipeline, and Google says it may retain that data for up to three years.

Google says it tries to filter personal information out of Gemini activity history, but explicitly does not guarantee it. Location and connected-app data are included in what may be used, which matters for anyone using Gemini alongside Maps, Gmail, or Drive.
report.impact: For regular users, this is a genuine improvement in granularity: you can now keep a working memory of past chats without donating that content to model training. But because training stays opt-out, the practical effect depends on whether people find the toggle — most won't, so Google's data pool stays large. For developers, the signal is that granular consent is becoming table stakes; anyone shipping an AI product with a single 'delete history or accept training' switch should expect the same scrutiny, particularly in the EU. For the industry, it pressures rivals to match granular controls and reframes the debate from 'do you train on us' to 'can we separate convenience from consent.' It does not stop data collection, only one downstream use of it.
report.tools: If you want privacy-preserving alternatives, try local runners like Ollama, LM Studio, or llama.cpp, which keep inference entirely on your machine. For cloud chat with weaker training defaults, look at DuckDuckGo AI Chat (anonymous proxy), Proton Lumo, and Mistral's Le Chat. Also audit the equivalent data controls in ChatGPT and Claude, and bookmark Google's My Activity dashboard to check what Gemini has already stored.
